Topics.Title: Introduction to the Standards Coverage View
Topics.Summary: Overview of the Standards Coverage view in PreseMaker, including its current development status and the headline summary it provides about a course's standards alignment.

Elements.Title: What the Standards Coverage View Is
Elements.BodyText: The Standards Coverage view is a feature in PreseMaker that shows how well your course materials cover the standards you have mapped, including whether coverage reaches the required cognitive depth.
Elements.Notes: This view is a newer feature and is currently labeled 'System in Development,' indicating it is still being refined.

Items.Text: It provides a unified place to evaluate both the breadth and depth of your course's standards alignment.
The 'System in Development' label signals that users should expect the feature to evolve over time.

Elements.Title: The Headline Summary
Elements.BodyText: At the top of the Standards Coverage view, a headline summarizes the overall alignment picture for the entire course at a glance.
Elements.Notes: For example, the headline might state what percentage of aligned standards are actually assessed and how many have a cognitive-depth gap.

Items.Text: The headline gives instructors an immediate, high-level sense of how complete their standards coverage is without reading every row.
It surfaces two key concerns at once: the proportion of standards that are assessed and the number of standards with a depth gap.

Elements.Title: How Standards Are Displayed as Rows
Elements.BodyText: Each mapped standard appears as its own row in the view, presenting several pieces of information together in a structured layout.

Items.Text: Each row shows the standard's code, its full statement, and its designated cognitive (Bloom's) level.
The row also displays counts of aligned assignments, quiz items, and activities, giving a quick inventory of supporting materials.
A Status indicator on each row communicates the current state of coverage for that standard.

Elements.Title: The Tiered Status System
Elements.BodyText: Rather than a numeric score or percentage bar, each standard receives one of a small set of tiered status labels that describe the quality of its coverage.
Elements.Notes: The key practical distinction is between 'practiced only' and 'assessed,' since assessment carries a higher level of accountability than practice alone.

Items.Text: 'Not aligned' means nothing has been mapped to the standard; 'not addressed' means it is mapped but no materials yet practice or assess it.
'Practiced only' means the standard is covered by an activity or assignment but no quiz item assesses it.
'Assessed' is the highest tier, meaning at least one assessment item covers the standard.

Elements.Title: Cognitive-Depth Checking Within the View
Elements.BodyText: The Standards Coverage view automatically flags any standard whose coverage is shallower than the cognitive level the standard itself demands, creating a visible depth-gap warning.
Elements.Notes: The required cognitive depth is determined by the standard's own Bloom's level, not by any external program setting.

Items.Text: A warning marker with a tooltip appears inline on the affected standard's row, making depth gaps easy to spot while scanning the list.
Depth-gap flags are also reflected in the headline summary, so the overall scale of the issue is visible immediately.
There is no separate button to run the check and no option to export a depth report; the check is built directly into the view.

Topics.Title: Understanding What the Coverage View Displays
Topics.Summary: Explanation of the information shown for each mapped standard, including its code, statement, cognitive level, aligned item counts, and overall status.

Elements.Title: The Standard Row Layout
Elements.BodyText: Each mapped standard appears as its own row in the Coverage view, consolidating all key information in one place.
Elements.Notes: This row-based layout allows instructors to scan all mapped standards at a glance without navigating away from the view.

Items.Text: Every row displays the standard's code, which serves as its unique identifier within the standards framework.
The full statement of the standard is shown alongside the code, providing the complete description of what learners are expected to know or do.
Counts of aligned assignments, quiz items, and activities are displayed directly on each row, giving a quick snapshot of how much material is tied to that standard.

Elements.Title: The Cognitive (Bloom's) Level Column
Elements.BodyText: Each standard row includes the cognitive level associated with that standard, drawn from Bloom's Taxonomy.
Elements.Notes: This level is set by the standard itself, not by any program-level configuration, and it serves as the benchmark against which coverage depth is measured.

Items.Text: The cognitive level indicates the depth of thinking the standard demands, such as remembering, applying, or evaluating.
Both standards and learning outcomes carry Bloom's levels, enabling a direct comparison between what is required and what is being taught or assessed.
This column is central to identifying whether course materials meet, exceed, or fall short of the intellectual rigor the standard requires.

Elements.Title: The Tiered Status Field
Elements.BodyText: Each standard is assigned one of a small set of status tiers rather than a numeric score, clearly categorizing how well it is currently covered.
Elements.Notes: The distinction between 'practiced only' and 'assessed' is particularly important, as practicing a skill through an activity does not carry the same evaluative weight as a formal quiz assessment.

Items.Text: 'Not aligned' means nothing in the course has been mapped to that standard.
'Not addressed' means the standard is mapped but no materials currently practice or assess it.
'Practiced only' means the standard is engaged through assignments or activities but is not covered by any quiz item.
'Assessed' means at least one quiz or assessment item directly covers the standard.

Elements.Title: The Coverage Headline Summary
Elements.BodyText: A headline at the top of the Coverage view summarizes the overall state of standards coverage across the entire course.
Elements.Notes: This summary gives instructors an immediate high-level picture before they examine individual standard rows in detail.

Items.Text: The headline reports what percentage of aligned standards are actually assessed, helping instructors gauge overall assessment completeness.
It also indicates how many standards have a cognitive-depth gap, flagging where coverage is shallower than the standard demands.
These two figures together allow instructors to prioritize which standards need the most urgent attention.

Elements.Title: The Inline Cognitive-Depth Gap Flag
Elements.BodyText: When a standard's coverage does not reach the cognitive depth its level requires, the row displays an inline warning marker.
Elements.Notes: There is no separate button to run a depth check and no option to export a depth report; the flag appears automatically as part of the Coverage view itself.

Items.Text: The warning marker appears directly on the standard's row, keeping the depth gap visible in context rather than in a separate report.
A tooltip on the marker provides additional detail about the nature of the depth gap.
The required depth is determined solely by the standard's own cognitive level, not by any external program or institutional setting.

Topics.Title: The Tiered Status System
Topics.Summary: Breakdown of the four status tiers — not aligned, not addressed, practiced only, and assessed — and the key distinction between practiced-only and assessed coverage.

Elements.Title: Overview of the Four Status Tiers
Elements.BodyText: Every mapped standard is assigned one of four discrete status tiers rather than a numeric score or percentage.
Elements.Notes: The tiered system provides a qualitative classification that makes it easy to see at a glance which standards need attention.

Items.Text: The four tiers are: not aligned, not addressed, practiced only, and assessed.
Each tier reflects a progressively deeper level of instructional engagement with the standard.
There are no percentage bars or numeric depth scores — status is categorical.

Elements.Title: Not Aligned
Elements.BodyText: A standard is marked 'not aligned' when no course materials have been mapped to it at all.

Items.Text: This is the baseline state indicating the standard has been included in the library but has no associated assignments, quiz items, or activities.
It signals that coverage work for this standard has not yet begun.

Elements.Title: Not Addressed
Elements.BodyText: A standard is marked 'not addressed' when it has been mapped to the course but no materials yet practice or assess it.
Elements.Notes: This tier distinguishes between the act of mapping a standard and actually delivering instruction against it.

Items.Text: Mapping alone is insufficient — materials must actively engage with the standard for its status to advance.
A 'not addressed' standard has been acknowledged in the course design but remains without any instructional or assessment coverage.

Elements.Title: Practiced Only
Elements.BodyText: A standard reaches 'practiced only' status when it is covered through an activity or assignment but has not yet been assessed by a quiz item.
Elements.Notes: This tier is meaningful because practice and assessment serve different instructional purposes — practice builds skill, while assessment verifies mastery.

Items.Text: Activities and assignments can move a standard from 'not addressed' to 'practiced only,' but they cannot raise it to 'assessed.'
A practiced-only standard is receiving instructional attention but lacks the formal verification that an assessment provides.
This tier often indicates a gap that should be resolved by adding appropriate quiz or assessment items.

Elements.Title: Assessed
Elements.BodyText: A standard achieves 'assessed' status when at least one quiz or assessment item directly covers it.

Items.Text: The 'assessed' tier is the highest status a standard can reach in the coverage view.
Reaching this tier means the standard has moved beyond practice into formal measurement of student mastery.
Even an assessed standard may still carry a cognitive-depth flag if the assessment item does not meet the standard's required Bloom's level.

Elements.Title: The Key Distinction: Practiced Only vs. Assessed
Elements.BodyText: The most instructionally significant boundary in the tiered system is the line between 'practiced only' and 'assessed.'
Elements.Notes: Understanding this distinction helps instructors prioritize which standards require additional quiz items versus which simply need more practice materials.

Items.Text: Practice through activities or assignments does not count as assessment — only dedicated quiz or assessment items elevate a standard to 'assessed.'
A standard that is practiced but not assessed means students have engaged with the content but mastery has not been formally verified.
Moving a standard from 'practiced only' to 'assessed' typically requires adding quiz questions that target the standard at the appropriate cognitive level.

Topics.Title: The Cognitive-Depth Check
Topics.Summary: How the coverage view flags standards whose alignment is shallower than the standard's required Bloom's level, including where the flag appears and how the required depth is determined.

Elements.Title: What a Cognitive-Depth Gap Is
Elements.BodyText: A cognitive-depth gap occurs when a standard's coverage is shallower than the cognitive level the standard itself demands.
Elements.Notes: Both standards and learning outcomes carry Bloom's taxonomy levels, making it possible to compare the depth of coverage against the depth the standard requires.

Items.Text: The coverage view compares the Bloom's level of aligned materials against the Bloom's level assigned to the standard.
If the materials address the standard at a lower cognitive level than required, the system identifies this mismatch as a depth gap.
A depth gap can exist even when a standard has aligned assignments, quiz items, or activities — quantity of coverage does not guarantee sufficient depth.

Elements.Title: How the Required Depth Is Determined
Elements.BodyText: The required cognitive depth is drawn directly from the standard's own assigned Bloom's level, not from any external program setting.

Items.Text: Each standard in the Standards Library carries a designated Bloom's taxonomy level as part of its definition.
The coverage view uses that standard-level Bloom's assignment as the benchmark for the depth check.
Instructors or administrators cannot override the required depth through a program or course setting — it is inherent to the standard itself.

Elements.Title: Where the Depth-Gap Flag Appears
Elements.BodyText: When a depth gap is detected, the flag surfaces in two places within the coverage view: inline on the standard's row and in the overall headline summary.
Elements.Notes: The inline flag takes the form of a warning marker with a tooltip, allowing instructors to identify the specific standard that is shallowly covered at a glance.

Items.Text: A warning marker with a tooltip appears directly on the affected standard's row, identifying the depth gap at the individual standard level.
The coverage view headline summarizes how many standards across the course have a cognitive-depth gap, giving an at-a-glance course-wide picture.
The flag is integrated into the existing coverage view and does not require any separate action to generate or display.

Elements.Title: What the Depth Check Is Not
Elements.BodyText: The cognitive-depth check is a built-in, automatic part of the coverage view rather than a separately triggered or exportable feature.
Elements.Notes: Understanding these boundaries helps instructors know where to look and what to expect from the tool.

Items.Text: There is no separate button to run the depth check — it operates continuously as part of the coverage view itself.
The system does not generate a standalone depth report, nor does it provide a numeric depth score or percentage bar for each standard.
There is no option to export the depth-gap findings as a spreadsheet or PDF.

Elements.Title: Relationship Between the Depth Flag and Tiered Status
Elements.BodyText: A cognitive-depth gap flag is distinct from a standard's tiered status and can appear alongside any status tier that involves some coverage.
Elements.Notes: A standard could carry an 'assessed' status yet still receive a depth-gap flag if the assessment items target a lower Bloom's level than the standard requires.

Items.Text: The tiered status — not aligned, not addressed, practiced only, or assessed — reflects whether and how a standard is covered, not the cognitive depth of that coverage.
A depth gap flag adds a second dimension of evaluation on top of the status tier, specifically targeting whether the cognitive level is sufficient.
Resolving a depth gap requires attention to the Bloom's level of materials, whereas improving a status tier may only require adding more aligned materials regardless of depth.

Topics.Title: Strengthening Shallow or Incomplete Coverage
Topics.Summary: Strategies for addressing depth gaps and unassessed standards by adding or upgrading course materials to meet the required cognitive level of each standard.

Elements.Title: Recognizing When Coverage Needs Strengthening
Elements.BodyText: Coverage gaps appear when a standard's status is 'not addressed,' 'practiced only,' or flagged with a depth gap warning.
Elements.Notes: A depth gap is flagged inline on the standard's row with a warning marker and tooltip, and is also summarized in the module headline.

Items.Text: A 'not addressed' status means the standard is mapped but no materials yet practice or assess it.
A 'practiced only' status means no quiz item currently assesses the standard, even if activities or assignments address it.
A depth gap flag indicates that existing coverage is at a lower Bloom's level than the standard itself requires.
The headline summary tells you at a glance how many standards have depth gaps across the entire course.

Elements.Title: Understanding the Required Cognitive Level
Elements.BodyText: The target cognitive depth for each standard comes directly from the standard's own assigned Bloom's level, not from any program-wide setting.
Elements.Notes: Because both standards and learning outcomes carry Bloom's levels, the system can compare them automatically to identify mismatches.

Items.Text: Each standard row displays its Bloom's level, making it clear what cognitive depth your materials must reach.
You cannot adjust the required depth threshold in settings; it is fixed by the standard's own cognitive classification.
Matching or exceeding the standard's Bloom's level is the criterion for resolving a depth gap.

Elements.Title: Moving a Standard from 'Practiced Only' to 'Assessed'
Elements.BodyText: The most direct way to close a 'practiced only' gap is to add at least one quiz item that is aligned to the standard.
Elements.Notes: The key distinction in the coverage view is between practice (activities or assignments) and formal assessment (quiz items); only the latter achieves 'assessed' status.

Items.Text: Adding a quiz question aligned to the standard promotes its status from 'practiced only' to 'assessed.'
The new quiz item must be mapped to the standard to be counted in the coverage view.
Even a single aligned quiz item is sufficient to change the status, though more items increase assessment robustness.

Elements.Title: Upgrading Materials to the Correct Bloom's Level
Elements.BodyText: When a depth gap is flagged, existing materials must be supplemented or replaced with content that targets the standard at its required Bloom's level.
Elements.Notes: For example, if a standard requires 'Analyze' but current quiz items only ask students to 'Remember' or 'Understand,' new higher-order questions must be added.

Items.Text: Review the Bloom's level shown on the flagged standard's row to identify exactly what cognitive demand is missing.
Add quiz questions, assignments, or activities written at or above the standard's required Bloom's level.
Upgrading an existing item means revising its cognitive demand — for instance, changing a recall question into an analysis or evaluation task.
Both quiz items and activities can contribute to resolving a depth gap, but only a quiz item will also resolve a 'practiced only' status.

Elements.Title: Addressing a 'Not Addressed' Standard
Elements.BodyText: A standard with 'not addressed' status requires the creation of new course materials from scratch, since nothing currently practices or assesses it.
Elements.Notes: This is the most significant coverage gap because the standard has been mapped to the course but no instructional or assessment activity yet targets it.

Items.Text: Start by adding at least one activity or assignment that gives students practice with the standard's content and skill.
Follow up by adding an aligned quiz item so the standard reaches 'assessed' status rather than remaining 'practiced only.'
Ensure all new materials are written at the Bloom's level the standard demands to avoid immediately triggering a depth gap flag.

Elements.Title: Verifying That Gaps Are Resolved
Elements.BodyText: After adding or upgrading materials, the coverage view updates each standard's status and depth-gap flag to reflect the new alignment.
Elements.Notes: Because there is no separate report to export or regenerate, verification happens by returning to the Standards Coverage view and checking the updated status rows and headline.

Items.Text: A resolved depth gap will no longer show the warning marker on the standard's row.
A standard that has moved to 'assessed' status will reflect the updated quiz item count in its row.
The headline summary percentage of assessed standards and the count of depth gaps will update to reflect all improvements made.
